section: The Observational Foundation: Longer, Denser, and Harmonised Monitoring
subsection: Extending the temporal record
claim_paragraph: Nutrient and hydrological studies converge on the same horizon. Year-round measurement of flow and concentration for at least several years on new sites is deemed necessary to set management priorities \parencite{Kladivko2001}, and long-term records are singled out to close water and nutrient balances and study legacy pools \parencite{Sharpley2019} and to disentangle land-management from climate-change effects, with the corollary that policy evaluation demands patience \parencite{Bauwe2020,Kelley2017,Gillingham2000,Lemke2011}. Smoothing year-to-year variability requires evaluating both phases of a rotation \parencite{Randall2003,Randall2005}, assessing responses on an annualised, multi-year basis \parencite{Waring2024,Pittelkow2017}, and freeing drainage-water-management yield effects from confounding \parencite{Cooke2012}; only long-term records across a range of climatic conditions, gathering plant, soil, and water measurements together, yield appropriate guidelines \parencite{RANDALL1995}. Data spanning at least a normal, a wet, and a dry year are needed to resolve losses and transport routes \parencite{vanderSalm2012}, and as long a record as possible is required for trend estimation because water quality may lag the management-driven change \parencite{Ulén2007}. Long records are equally the only way to detect slow processes---soil organic-carbon recovery \parencite{Kumar2014}, discharge-driven organic-matter export \parencite{Manninen2023}, and whether drainage-induced soil evolution continues or stabilises over decades **[CITATION CHECKED: Frankl2023]**. Record length alone is insufficient: robust seasonal conclusions require year-round coverage, especially in the non-growing season \parencite{Klaiber2020,VanEsbroeck2016}, high-frequency records without gaps and instruments checked as often as possible \parencite{Hodaj2017}, and monitoring timed to infrastructure interventions such as drain repair \parencite{Wesström2015}.

section: The Observational Foundation: Longer, Denser, and Harmonised Monitoring
subsection: Tracers, isotopes, and source apportionment
claim_paragraph: Measurement and tracing techniques are repeatedly identified as the means to resolve pathways that bulk flow-and-concentration records leave ambiguous. \textcite{Williams2022} call for higher-frequency (sub-daily to daily) measurements, further work on groundwater dynamics in dissolved-P transport, and more comprehensive source-apportionment methods. Water- and nitrate-isotope approaches are advanced to quantify processes directly: coupling water and nitrate oxygen isotopes and quantifying the $\delta^{18}$O of nitrification-derived nitrate to constrain evaporative enrichment \parencite{Hu2024}, monitoring nitrate concentrations and isotopic compositions with multiple tracers across topsoil, drains, and ditches to characterise the soil contribution to river nitrate \parencite{Briand2017}, and boron isotopes to strengthen contaminant tracing around feedlots and fields **[CITATION CHECKED: Komor1997]**. High-frequency tracer measurements are urged to quantify water ages and represent both celerities and velocities \parencite{Williams2021}, alongside event sampling and bulk-soil-water isotopes to constrain young-water fractions \parencite{DimitrovaPetrova2020}, high-resolution specific conductance for end-member mixing \parencite{Kronholm2015,Schilling2019}, and conservative-tracer or water-isotope studies to partition quick flow and baseflow \parencite{Frederiksen2023}. Explicit pathway partitioning--- reporting surface-inlet presence and splitting water and nutrient loads by pathway via before-after control-impact designs, hydrograph separation, or tracers \parencite{Flores2021}, evaluating overland-flow versus tile-flow contributions \parencite{Kokulan2019}, and verifying groundwater flow paths and plant water sources with stable isotopes \parencite{Islam2022,YliHalla2022}---recurs throughout. The role of groundwater outflow in nutrient loading is flagged as under-quantified and in need of dedicated measurement and modelling \parencite{Turunen2013,Jokinen2024,Barkle2021}, and finer temporal analyses of the flow--concentration relationship, including detailed storm-hydrograph separation, are needed to test event-scale hypotheses \parencite{Lagzdins2015,Danalatos2022,Kladivko2004}.

section: The Observational Foundation: Longer, Denser, and Harmonised Monitoring
subsection: Broadening spatial and geographic scope
claim_paragraph: A second frontier is testing whether site-specific findings hold across other soils, climates, crops, and management regimes. Authors repeatedly defer broad adoption until similar data are collected from further sites and years \parencite{Menegaz2025,Zimmerman2017b,Terrado2015}, from additional agro-ecological zones \parencite{Ali2001}, from other settings for practices such as the two-stage ditch \parencite{Hodaj2017}, and from adverse or compacted conditions where a technology's merit is untested \parencite{Bigelow2001}. The most explicit prescription is that controlled-drainage and subirrigation studies be conducted outside the U.S. Midwest and Canada across diverse climates, crops, and soils, and--- crucially for generalisation---that site characterisation (slope, particle-size distribution by horizon, hydraulic conductivity, drainage class, and moisture) be reported with measures of variability \parencite{Singh2022b}. Repetition at larger scales and on contrasting soils is stressed as a key modulating factor \parencite{Bilotta2008,Goeken2015}, including for process studies such as earthworm activity on soils of differing texture and rainfall \parencite{Nuutinen2001,Nuutinen2011}. Climate-focused transferability demands high-resolution scenarios and multi-model uncertainty analysis at additional sites **[CITATION CHECKED: Rasmussen2018]**, and testing across regions, soils, and climates recurs throughout as the precondition for localised design guidance \parencite{Singh2020b,Malota2024,Salazar2008,Holbak2021}. At the level of synthesis, robust conclusions will require geographically diverse and methodologically harmonised studies so that meta-analyses can disentangle management effects \parencite{Wu2025}.

section: The Observational Foundation: Longer, Denser, and Harmonised Monitoring
subsection: Experimental design for detectable effects
claim_paragraph: Longer, standardised records are useful only if the design can resolve the effect sought. \textcite{Schilling2013} specify the ingredients for paired-basin detection: establishing a suitable correlation among paired basins across climates, restricting paired sampling to the March--July high-flow period, delaying post-treatment monitoring to enhance the chance of detecting change, and adopting practices capable of achieving at least the minimum detectable change. Effects should be assessed simultaneously at multiple scales, from field to watershed \parencite{Sunohara2016}, paired with within-field and within-plot studies to elucidate the mechanistic processes of export and additional field-scale studies within high-export sub-watersheds \parencite{Irvine2019}. Larger, more representative trial areas are sought to test effective-yield formulas \parencite{Xin2016c} and to refine tracer-based ($^{15}$N) loss observation \parencite{Xiong2025}, and mesocosms are proposed to quantify nutrient-loss responses to management change under controlled conditions \parencite{Loper2024}. Because field-scale drainage trials are typically unreplicated, several authors treat the analysis itself as an open question: whether beta distributions, time series, or new methods best analyse unreplicated paired experiments \parencite{Pagliari2021}, and whether directed hypothesis tests should be favoured over replicate spatial analyses \parencite{Andrus2014}. Where replication is feasible, replicated field experiments, matched instrumentation, and improved sampling designs are recommended to support statistical inference **[CITATION CHECKED: Wamono2016b]**. Together these design refinements define the bridge between a lengthening, harmonised observational record and the detectable, transferable conclusions the rest of the field depends upon.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Instrumentation and measurement-method validation
claim_paragraph: Because model validation is only as sound as the data feeding it, uncalibrated flow structures and drifting sensors can masquerade as model inadequacy. In-house calibration of flow-measurement structures is recommended repeatedly: weir calibration for individual applications \parencite{Christianson2019,Napierala2023}, in-house calibrations representing field flow conditions for control structures \parencite{Katuwal2024}, stage--discharge equations developed before monitoring for cylindrical structures \parencite{BinShokrana2021}, and post-hoc sensor calibration against grab samples during tracer tests \parencite{deOliveira2023b}. Emerging technologies carry explicit validation requirements: a computer-vision flow method needs testing under variable real-world conditions with the Manning--Strickler equation to compensate for uneven velocities \parencite{Young2023}, hybrid RTK--rotating-laser systems address less-than-ideal survey conditions \parencite{Freeland2014}, and sensor design and scintillometer humidity-stability effects require refinement **[CITATION CHECKED: Enamorado2007]**. Hydraulic-loss characterisation in drainage conduits remains conspicuously incomplete, limiting design-equation realism: head loss in corrugated-pipe junctions and manholes under free-surface flow \parencite{Bayat2011}, friction loss and transitional cavity-flow conditions \parencite{Nédélec2008}, declining-bend slope effects on air discharge \parencite{Gurklys2008}, appropriate Manning coefficients for design \parencite{Kouchakzadeh2011}, and strain-gauge characterisation of non-linear HDPE-pipe behaviour \parencite{Gaj2021}. The consistent message across the modelling frontier is that the next decade of progress depends less on new equations than on sustained, well-instrumented, and openly reported field campaigns needed to test the equations already in hand.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Broadening the empirical basis for validation
claim_paragraph: A recurring, more ambitious hypothesis is that empirical coefficients could be replaced with functions of measurable site attributes. \textcite{Li2006} commit to testing across climate zones, soils, and management while anticipating that coefficient constants might become functions of soil texture, converting site-specific tuning into transferable structure; \textcite{Chelil2022} cast the same concern as spatial robustness, arguing that additional fields are needed to confirm that parameters such as nitrate-transfer velocities are transferable rather than calibration artefacts. Verification at independent sites is treated as a precondition, not optional confirmation \parencite{Azevedo1997,Qi2015,Kalita1998,Sadhukhan2019b}, with inconsistencies producing conflicting parameter values resolved first \parencite{Dar2022} and empirical codes transferred only through re-parameterisation with local soil, geology, crop, and climate data, or region-specific coefficients where reference values exist \parencite{Azevedo1997,FathAllah2025,Rijal2013}. The open question is how much local data such transfer requires. Extending validation across the climatic and design envelope is closely related: humid-region models need testing under semi-arid regimes and after prolonged dry spells \parencite{Prasher1996}, longer monitoring records give firmer conclusions \parencite{Ebrahimian2011,Grazhdani1996}, and design geometry demands experiments at spacings wider than 30~m and regional answers on drainage-efficiency loss and design storms \parencite{Mathew2001,Wiskow2003,MULLER1988}. Long simulations of 50--100 years are argued necessary to judge whether a design meets its criteria **[CITATION CHECKED: Häggblom2019]**. Portability, in short, is a hypothesis to be tested, not a property to be presumed \parencite{Hornbuckle2012,Shipitalo2016,Yousfi2014}.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Field and process data still needed to constrain models
claim_paragraph: Phosphorus is similarly data-limited, and its dominant pathway---preferential flow---is the hardest to observe. Many phosphorus-index factors need investigation of their effect on field-to-stream transfer, and index rankings must be shown to reflect actual transfer risk \parencite{Bechmann2007,Beauchemin2003}. Confirming P-movement trends requires quantitative tracer measurement of preferential flow \parencite{Salazar2011,Tiemeyer2009}, structural deficiencies around surface runoff and tile P transport need repair \parencite{Apostel2021}, and accurate capture of flashy export demands automated samplers, real-time sensors, and high-resolution topographic survey of ditch sediment before and after storms \parencite{Dialameh2022,Warsta2014}. Supporting empirical work includes further testing of CaCl$_2$-P as a dissolved-reactive-P estimator \parencite{McDowell2001b}, regression models linking drainage parameters to P losses \parencite{Morrison2013}, tests using actual effluent under fluctuating flow \parencite{Sanford2016}, and long-term monitoring of P sources **[CITATION CHECKED: Jia2012]**. Sampling design is itself a constraint: weekly sampling may be needed to capture nitrate spikes before they pass below suction-cup samplers \parencite{Zotarelli2007}, more frequent early-season and summer-event sampling is advised \parencite{Kalita1998,Tiemeyer2009}, and denser sampling geometry sharpens semi-variograms and optimal sampling density \parencite{GALLICHAND1992,Upadhyay2019}.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Model structure, coupling, and machine learning
claim_paragraph: Beyond recalibration, structural refinements and integrative strategies are judged necessary. Coupling complementary models is a common, largely untested proposal: linking biogeochemical to spatial hydrological models such as SWAT or MIKE~SHE for regional prediction \parencite{Li2006}, coupling nitrate-transport and drainage models with variational assimilation of spring-fertilisation information \parencite{Chelil2022}, and integrated use of more than one model as more practical than a single code \parencite{Singh2019b,Apostel2021}. Machine-learning models raise their own validation requirements the literature is only beginning to confront: hyperparameter tuning and diverse training data for drain detection \parencite{Song2021}, neural networks needing training that includes extreme situations and periodic retraining \parencite{Yang2000}, and machine-learning surrogates trained across diverse climatic and hydrogeological conditions with transient processes and real-time control \parencite{Lei2026,Schneider2022}. Process-model deficiencies are named directly---detailed site characterisation, added non-linear regression dependences, and improved submodels for mineralisation, crop N uptake, and growth under N limitation \parencite{Ahuja2007,Ikenberry2017}, with added complexity the price of predicting snowmelt-thaw drainage timing \parencite{Feyereisen2007}. Physical and analytical refinements form a rich set of concrete proposals: numerical models incorporating anisotropy and varying bottom slopes verified against analytical solutions **[CITATION CHECKED: Lin2025]**, reanalysis with the Laplace rather than Boussinesq equation \parencite{Bouarfa2000}, recession equations extended to spatially varying properties \parencite{Cooke2001}, three-dimensional treatment at heterogeneous sites \parencite{Mohanty1997}, distinct mixing-layer depths and partition coefficients for solute transport \parencite{Shalit1996}, reconsidered deep-percolation and shallow-water-table assumptions \parencite{Kolars2019}, and strengthened index-system construction with additional soil indicators \parencite{Hou2018}.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Nutrient routines, cold-season, and groundwater coupling
claim_paragraph: Soil N-process representation is repeatedly the weakest link. Priorities include improving nitrification, denitrification, and mineralisation within a better hydrology framework \parencite{Smith2020,Fang2012,Hu2007}, and recurring RZWQM agendas---subsurface lateral flow below tiles, simulated soybean N fixation, improved plant N uptake, and reduced winter nitrification \parencite{Ma2007,Ma2008,Ma2001,Bakhsh2004}---together with revised winter processes in the PNM model **[CITATION CHECKED: Marjerison2016]** and a more physically based tile-nitrate model using ``soft data'' and a passive humus pool \parencite{Qi2025}. Cold-season representation is singled out as inadequate: better freeze/thaw and spring-thaw algorithms \parencite{Feyereisen2006b}, DRAINMOD-N improvement for freezing seasons \parencite{Yang2007,Saadat2020,Jiang2020}, a frozen-soil impedance factor and calibratable snow--rain threshold for RZ-SHAW \parencite{Li2024b}, and continued RZWQM winter development \parencite{Ahmed2007b,Motarjemi2021}. Coupling drainage models to groundwater is a distinct need: SWAT-MODFLOW-RT3D for reactive transport once salinity is incorporated \parencite{Addab2022}, water-table-fluctuation and groundwater--surface-water exchange in SWAT to represent riparian nitrate retention \parencite{Hoang2017}, joint spatial variation in leaching and reduction across systems \parencite{Hojberg2017}, and defensible water balances splitting artificial drainage from groundwater flow \parencite{Barkle2021,Elsayed2023,Yang2008}. In arid settings, coupling of water and salt dynamics with unsaturated models, root-growth modules, and large-dataset validation is pressed \parencite{Ebrahimian2015,Sarangi2006,Han2025,Liu2022,Guo2025}.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Coupled hydraulics, seepage, and soil heterogeneity
claim_paragraph: Nearly every modelling study attributes residual error to unresolved heterogeneity in hydraulic properties, especially conductivity. Authors seek detailed representation of macropores, fractures, and sand lenses with specific storage and residual saturation \parencite{DeSchepper2017}, depth-varying and dual-porosity parameterisations in layered and paddy soils \parencite{Wesström2003,Karandish2018}, and denser, depth-resolved sampling---at least one conductivity measurement per hectare with post-construction verification **[CITATION CHECKED: PalaciosVélez2004]**, more transect points \parencite{Messing2006}, and horizontal as well as vertical conductivities with hydrophobicity and hysteresis \parencite{Tähtikarhu2025}. Anisotropy and long-term property change form a related sub-frontier \parencite{Akis2015,Moustafa1998,Koivusalo1999}, and accurate saturated conductivity and drainage-volume/upward-flux relationships, supported by SSURGO-linked subsoil porosity, are emphasised as model inputs \parencite{DeBoer2006,Schilling2015,DeSchepper2015}. Closing the water balance---particularly seepage and groundwater exchange---remains persistent: lateral seepage should vary during simulation \parencite{Feng2018}, groundwater contributions could enter through double- or residual-storage models \parencite{DaneshYazdi2016}, and groundwater-table data in objective functions would sharpen inverse recovery of soil properties \parencite{Sedaghatdoost2018,Sedaghatdoost2019}. Improved calibration strategy is widely urged---parameter-estimation software and multiple conceptual models \parencite{Boico2022}, pilot-point conductivity fields with proxy machine-learning predictions \parencite{Schneider2022}, Kling--Gupta objective functions \parencite{Brighenti2023}, and transient tests of steady-state assumptions \parencite{Schilling2022,Gates2002,Burkhalter2006}. Contemporary needs also span unsaturated modules for disconnected groundwater \parencite{Kompanizare2024}, independent layer-to-layer drainage methods under preferential flow \parencite{Ojeda2018}, and dynamic frozen-soil models with measured structure \parencite{Ulén2016}.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Preferential and macropore flow representation
claim_paragraph: The representation of preferential flow is perhaps the most frequently cited frontier, the recurring theme being that its contribution to drains must be characterised as a function of soil type, water content, and practice before models extrapolate. \textcite{Gaillot2023} and \textcite{Fox2004} call for mechanistic characterisation of macropore--drain connectivity and of the ``express fraction'' under varying saturation above the drain, and \textcite{Askar2020} stress that rigorous testing of DRAINMOD's empirical macropore approach requires water-table-depth measurements alongside drainage and runoff, direct macropore-flow inputs, and crack geometry and dynamics. Process improvements span better matrix--macropore partitioning calibrated against sub-hourly drainage in RZWQM2 \parencite{Li2023d}, dynamic connectivity or effective macroporosity at watershed scale \parencite{Poon2021}, micropore diffusion and site-specific conductivities in dual-permeability descriptions \parencite{Villholth1998,Villholth1998b}, hysteresis and biopore-flow initiation \parencite{Holbak2021}, manure-driven macropore development \parencite{Zhao2001}, crack re-establishment in EPIC \parencite{Wang2022}, and calibrated macropore conductivity in three-dimensional dual-permeability models \parencite{Varvaris2018}. Direct pathway identification is repeatedly urged---ground-penetrating radar and tracers with explicit flowpath representation \parencite{Tähtikarhu2025,Salo2017}, dye-staining of routes reaching tile lines \parencite{Nielsen2015}, and near-surface pathway characterisation \parencite{Frey2012,Allaire2011}. Central quantitative questions remain the fraction of phosphorus and solutes delivered via preferential versus matrix flow \parencite{King2015,Williams2016}, the range of macropore flows across soils and management \parencite{Reid2012}, and by-pass flow through cracks for full-year application **[CITATION CHECKED: Ruark2009]**. Runoff simulation under crusting, cracking, and preferential flow \parencite{Smith2020}, explicit representation of actual drain configuration \parencite{Stamm2002}, temporal variability in hydrological-pathway activation for cracking clays \parencite{Kokulan2019}, and seasonal, time-dependent shrink--swell and hydraulic-conductivity measurement \parencite{Boivin2006,Chelil2022b,Jeantet2021} complete this agenda.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Coupled hydraulics, seepage, and soil heterogeneity
claim_paragraph: A recurrent structural gap is the absence of models coupling soil pore-water flow with surface flow inside drains and ditches. \textcite{Xin2016b} call for coupling drain surface water with pore-water flow to represent the time-varying head around the drain, and \textcite{Nousiainen2015} propose simulating in-pipe flow to capture pressurisation and clogging, adding open-ditch networks. Pressurised-flow dynamics are a specific frontier: coupling pipes to the water table could introduce a validated temporary-retention function beyond design capacity \parencite{Henine2010,Henine2014}, with pressurised periods analysed separately from pressure-transducer data \parencite{Saadat2018}. Entrance resistance, near-drain pressure heads, and rapid trench-backfill versus slower inter-trench transport remain unresolved for heterogeneous systems \parencite{Messing2006,Rimidis2003}, and model dimensionality is itself a question---two- or three-dimensional treatment of sloping fields, collectors, and regional management \parencite{Alakukku2010,FIPPS1989,Carlier2007,Mohanty1998}---within broader integrating frameworks **[CITATION CHECKED: SAVABI1993]**.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Calibration, sensitivity analysis, and uncertainty
claim_paragraph: How models are calibrated and their parameters interrogated is inseparable from validity. Multiobjective frameworks integrating statistical and graphical diagnostics tailored to the hydrological system are advocated \parencite{Bruhn2025}, reliable soil-hydraulic data for the drain layer is emphasised with interacting parameters calibrated and negligible ones fixed \parencite{Wang2006}, and independent calibration against observed discharge is recommended so interception and storage are not conflated with conductivity and drainable porosity \parencite{Henine2022}. Pedotransfer estimates such as Rosetta conductivity should be used cautiously, with further calibration so both water-table depth and discharge are simulated \parencite{Malota2022,Timalsina2023}. A common thread is identifiability---separating parameters that genuinely act from those merely correlated. Automated and global approaches are widely urged: automatic calibration with ensemble Kalman filtering for parameter identification **[CITATION CHECKED: Sadhukhan2019b]**, global sensitivity analysis to capture interactions that local one-at-a-time methods miss \parencite{Timalsina2023,Chelil2022,Kacimov2000}, established bounds for the SWAT sensitivity adjustment factor \parencite{Moriasi2013b}, and spatially distributed streambed conductance with exchange fluxes as calibration targets and drainage proxies \parencite{Karan2021}. Explicit uncertainty treatment is a distinct, underdeveloped frontier: propagation of parameter and measurement error \parencite{Alzraiee2013b}, the role of input-data and weather-data quality \parencite{Upadhyay2019,Tao2021}, explicit estimation of P-model prediction accuracy \parencite{Radcliffe2015,Beauchemin2003}, structural uncertainty via multiple water-quality models \parencite{Kujawa2020}, probabilistic drainage-water-management effectiveness \parencite{Shedekar2021}, independent evaluation against withheld data \parencite{Schoups2005}, and better statistical treatment of unreplicated paired experiments \parencite{Pagliari2021,Andrus2014}. The recurring message is that models are too often reported as point predictions when their inputs warrant propagated bounds.

section: Advancing Process-Based Drainage and Water-Quality Models
subsection: Broadening the empirical basis for validation
claim_paragraph: The most frequently articulated need is validation data spanning a wider range of conditions than any single study can supply. \textcite{Youssef2006} describe rigorous field testing across differing management, soils, and climates as a need common to nearly all simulation models, and warn that assumptions must be re-verified whenever a code is transferred to a new area \parencite{Kelleners2000}; similar calls for broader-condition testing, sensitivity analysis, and parameter refinement recur for pesticide, salt, and flow models **[CITATION CHECKED: Yang2008b]**. Models are repeatedly reported as requiring testing over longer periods and additional soil types \parencite{Salazar2009,Li2026}, and their effectiveness under new controlled-drainage or erosion conditions is judged critically needed before higher credibility can be claimed \parencite{Negm2017,Turunen2020}.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment Technologies
subsection: Aging, longevity, clogging, subsidence, and construction
claim_paragraph: The multi-decadal service life and physical stability of treatment structures are among the least-studied dimensions. \textcite{Ghane2018} recommend longer study of woodchip particle-size reduction, investigation of whether woodchip carbon becomes recalcitrant to the point of inefficiency before particle-size reduction throttles flow, and studies beyond ten years. \textcite{Christianson2020} similarly call for long-term documentation of biofilm formation, siltation, wood decay, and the effects of a decreasing carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and increasing lignocellulose index, to inform woodchip-recharge thresholds; long-term ($>$8~yr) field programmes were underway to establish efficacy \parencite{Greenan2009}, and spatiotemporal removal should be evaluated across normal, wet, and drought years alongside woodchip C:N measurements \parencite{Hartfiel2023b}. Estimating replacement interval and cost depends on performance, lifespan, and residue cost, with pre-measured feedstock volumes proposed to control construction-method effects \parencite{Kohn2023}. Chemical clogging is mechanistically unresolved and needs simulation models for prevention \parencite{Guo2020,Guo2021}. Subsidence monitoring is a new methodological frontier: \textcite{Christianson2025b} propose applying a LiDAR method at additional sites---especially immediately after construction---to build subsidence time series and assess targeted inlet recharge. Sediment management at construction is itself a design frontier: \textcite{Feyereisen2023} plan to weigh the opposing effects of bypass flow and nitrate removal in a sediment-exclusion system and advise pre-construction investigation of sedimentation sources. Network-scale diagnostics also need extension---higher-pressure air injection and time-domain electromagnetic resistivity monitoring for large drainage networks **[CITATION CHECKED: Henine2021]**.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment Technologies
subsection: Phosphorus-removal media and filter design
claim_paragraph: Phosphorus-sorption materials (PSMs) constitute one of the most heavily populated gap areas, spanning selection, longevity, regeneration, and hydraulic integration. \textcite{Li2020} argue that adsorbent choice must weigh phosphorus concentration, interfering ions, temperature, flow rate, and sediment load; prioritise selectivity at neutral pH; be testable for reuse and recovery; and be economical at field scale. \textcite{Mendes2022} add that the apparently synergistic retention mechanism of filter media at high flow rates is unknown and that regeneration of spent media should be pursued. Iron- and steel-based media dominate specific proposals: optimising an iron-oxyhydroxide regeneration process and evaluating low-cost goethite such as bog iron ore \parencite{Allred2017}; determining minimum contact time for zero-valent iron via higher-flow column and isotherm tests \parencite{Allred2014}; regenerating steel by-products by alkaline washing \parencite{Hua2016}; connecting a steel-slag filter to a bioreactor only after the initial DOC flush and mixing fine steel to preserve conductivity \parencite{Sellner2019b}; optimising removal, retention time, slag mass, and cost \parencite{Wang2020d}; controlling sediment influx and improving flow distribution \parencite{Shedekar2020}; and recognising that ligand-exchange PSMs suit tile drainage only where structures allow high-frequency media replacement (every 4--6 months) **[CITATION CHECKED: Penn2020]**. Fly-ash and pellet media raise saturation-timing questions---saturation time must be quantified before field use so pellets are replaced before shifting from phosphorus sink to source \parencite{Li2017,Li2018b}---and filter blends remain unoptimised with respect to media configuration, contact time, and high-flow contact \parencite{Agrawal2011,Agrawal2011b,Kumari2025,Kankarej2023}. Integrated woodchip-plus-PSM designs need multi-scale, multiyear evaluation of removal effectiveness, media placement, lifespan, and regeneration \parencite{Husk2018}.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment Technologies
subsection: Enhancing the microbial engine
claim_paragraph: Rational manipulation presupposes mechanistic understanding of the resident community, which is incomplete. \textcite{Hartfiel2022} argue that bioreactor microbiome study should draw on soil and wetland ecology; that controls on cellulose- and lignin-metabolism genes warrant attention; that dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium and anammox have been observed but understudied; and that varying substrates to select for differing communities is a promising route to more consistent performance and reduced by-product formation---the mechanism by which HRT shapes the community, and thereby by-product production, being a specific gap. Complementary needs include managing bed pH for acidic drainage and conceptualising regional controls on in-bed nitrogen removal \parencite{Bock2018}, routine monitoring of nitrite to avoid its accumulation in effluent \parencite{Kouanda2021}, and characterising the selective pressure of oxygen versus nitrate load on community assembly **[CITATION CHECKED: Schaefer2021]**. The emissions accounting of these by-products is treated in the consequences synthesis; here they define a design and monitoring constraint.

section: Salinity, Reclamation, and Drainage-Water Reuse in Arid and Irrigated Systems
subsection: Salt-leaching dynamics and long-term reclamation trajectories
claim_paragraph: The recurring message is temporal: meaningful salt reduction often accrues so slowly that short observation windows systematically underestimate long-term benefit, and only extended drainage with sustained monitoring resolves the true trajectory \parencite{Almen2021,Daigh2025}. subsection: Economics, incentives, and cost-effectiveness

section: Conclusions
subsection: (no subsections)
claim_paragraph: The second priority is strengthened and validated model components. Because field trials cannot span every combination of practice, soil, and climate, process-based drainage and water-quality models are expected to carry much of the predictive burden; yet their credibility is constrained less by their formulation than by the narrowness of the conditions under which they have been tested. Validation across a wider envelope, the replacement of empirical coefficients with functions of measurable site attributes, and the process-level measurements needed to constrain the least mature routines--- denitrification and the nitrogen cycle, phosphorus and its dominant preferential-flow pathway, cold-season dynamics, and coupled seepage and groundwater exchange---are near-universal priorities \parencite{Youssef2006,Radcliffe2015}. So too are explicit attention to identifiability and uncertainty, so that models are reported with propagated bounds rather than as point predictions, and the disciplined integration of machine learning and coupled model structures, whose own validation requirements the field is only beginning to confront. section: Introduction
subsection: (no subsections)
claim_paragraph: The hydrologic changes wrought by drainage are double-edged. Relative to undrained or surface-drained land, improved subsurface drainage generally reduces surface runoff, peak flow, sediment, and particulate phosphorus, yet it opens an efficient conduit for nitrate, coupling tile-drained cropland to hypoxia in the Gulf of Mexico and to the eutrophication of inland waters \parencite{FAUSEY1995,SKAGGS1994,THOMAS1995,Gramlich2018,Raymond2012}. The once-common presumption that the soil profile filters subsurface water into a ``clean'' pathway has been overturned: a small volume of hydraulically active macropores delivers phosphorus, sediment, and conservative tracers to drains within hours of application or rainfall \parencite{Pease2018}. At the same time drainage remains a foundational production technology that raises yields on excess-water-stressed soils, reclaims saline and waterlogged land, and returns favourable financial and social benefits **[CITATION CHECKED: Yang2025]**. Reconciling these competing outcomes---water-quality protection against agronomic and economic gain---is the defining management challenge of drained agriculture.

section: Drainage Hydrology: Flow Pathways, Regime, and Scaling
subsection: Scale Dependence, Homogenization, and Travel Times
claim_paragraph: Artificial drainage homogenises catchment response and reduces the scale dependence of hydrologic signatures. Non-tiled Iowa watersheds show decreasing area-normalized peak discharge and increasing baseflow ratio with scale, whereas tiled basins behave scale-invariantly; within-basin variability in recession coefficients declines as drained fraction rises, and the tiled/non-tiled distinction disappears above roughly 2200~km$^2$ \parencite{BolandBrien2014}. In Minnesota's Redwood basin, mean travel time fell 41\% (77 to 45~d), year-to-year variability was reduced, and travel time became independent of catchment size above about 200~km$^2$ \parencite{DaneshYazdi2016}, with streamflow dynamics becoming more linear after 1976 despite little change in precipitation \parencite{FoufoulaGeorgiou2015}. Isotope work in a UK catchment found short mean transit times ($<$1~yr, faster in artificial drains) and concluded that drainage homogenised distributed responses **[CITATION CHECKED: DimitrovaPetrova2020]**, and an Indiana watershed behaved as an effectively homogeneous unit describable by a single exponential travel-time distribution with a 2--3~d mean \parencite{Basu2010}; even so, tile contributions remained detectable beyond 16{,}000~km$^2$ in the Boone River \parencite{Schilling2019}.

section: Drainage Hydrology: Flow Pathways, Regime, and Scaling
subsection: Modification of the Flow Regime
claim_paragraph: Flashiness responds to drainage in a soil- and slope-dependent way. A global meta-analysis of 464 watersheds found overall flashiness (Richards--Baker Index) similar regardless of drainage extent but diverging by setting: in flat watersheds ($<$2\% slope) medium/high drainage raised the index, whereas in sloping watersheds low extent had the highest, with drainage extent correlating positively with agricultural land use and clay content and negatively with slope \parencite{Zhou2025}. Field-scale Iowa simulations showed drainage decreased flashiness for low-conductivity soils and increased it for high-conductivity soils, homogenising response with an optimal spacing near 15~m **[CITATION CHECKED: Sloan2016]**, while Ohio modelling found overall flashiness decreased with tiles, minimised near 50~m spacing \parencite{Rathore2025}. Across 30 Nordic--Baltic catchments, flashiness related negatively to baseflow index and positively to drained share and intensity, and computing it from hourly rather than daily discharge increased it nearly threefold \parencite{Deelstra2014,Deelstra2014b}. At the regime scale, drainage significantly increased streamflow-drought duration and intensity while reducing frequency, each 10\% increase in tile-drained area lengthening drought duration by 0.03~d, raising intensity 12\%, and lowering frequency 0.10 events~yr$^{-1}$ \parencite{Adelsperger2024}. Indiana trend analysis found increasing low- and medium-flow trends with weakened precipitation linkage in heavily drained areas \parencite{Kumar2009}, although a synthesis of seven Midwestern rivers concluded that inter-annual variability in streamflow and baseflow was controlled primarily by current- and previous-year precipitation \parencite{Baeumler2020}.

section: Drainage Hydrology: Flow Pathways, Regime, and Scaling
subsection: Repartitioning of Water Relative to Undrained Land
claim_paragraph: At the field-water-balance scale, the tile drain, not the soil surface, is usually the principal conduit in humid settings. In Indiana, surface runoff was only 1--10\% of annual precipitation versus 26--45\% for subsurface drainage (simulated balance 7\% runoff, 34\% drain flow, 51\% evapotranspiration), with all ponding generated by saturation excess \parencite{Saadat2020}. Iowa pothole modelling found tile discharge and evapotranspiration accounting for 52.4\% and 47.5\% of precipitation \parencite{Amado2018,Martin2019}, and UK field drains were the dominant pathway transferring runoff and most sediment to the stream, responding in every monitored event \parencite{Deasy2009}. The direction of these shifts is texture-dependent: on sandy loams subsurface drainage minimised runoff and total-phosphorus loss whereas the reverse held on clay loam, phosphorus speciation being mainly a function of soil texture \parencite{Eastman2010}. Mechanistically, good drainage increases infiltration and lowers solute concentrations in surface runoff **[CITATION CHECKED: Tao2017]**, and by lowering the water table it limits saturation-excess runoff and surface sealing \parencite{Augeard2005}.

section: Nitrate Export: Magnitudes and Biophysical Controls
subsection: Concentration--discharge behaviour, sources, and denitrification
claim_paragraph: Dual-isotope studies indicate that drainage nitrate is often derived largely from organic sources (manure and soil organic matter) via nitrification, with denitrification not always dominant. In Ontario, $\delta^{15}$N and $\delta^{18}$O relationships lacked the 2:1 denitrification slope, pointing to organic sources and continued nitrification through all seasons \parencite{Smith2011,Smith2011b}, and rapid nitrification of applied ammonium ($>90\%$ within $72$~h) supplies ready nitrate for leaching \parencite{Hu2024}. Where denitrification is active it is detectable: along Polish flow paths nitrate declined while sulfate, excess N$_2$, $\delta^{15}$N, and $\delta^{18}$O increased \parencite{Dragon2016}, and nested French watersheds implied $34$--$82\%$ nitrate retention dominated by underground denitrification \parencite{Billy2011,Billy2013}. In Iowa drainageways, denitrification in slowly permeable soils could remove essentially all upland groundwater nitrate, functioning as a natural treatment system **[CITATION CHECKED: Cambardella1999]**. Yet where drains intercept water before it reaches these attenuating zones, export is high: tile discharge is dominated by pre-event water---three-component separation gave $65\%$ groundwater and $29\%$ shallow soil water---yet tile drains carried the highest NO$_3$-N of any source and contributed over $99\%$ of watershed nitrate export \parencite{Williams2022,Grose2022}.

section: Nitrate Export: Magnitudes and Biophysical Controls
subsection: Subsurface drainage as the dominant nitrogen pathway
claim_paragraph: Multiple independent studies establish that in tile-drained landscapes the subsurface pathway carries most of the nitrogen. In intensively monitored Norwegian catchments, subsurface drainage carried $76$--$91\%$ of runoff and $87$--$95\%$ of total-N (TN) loss, with drainage TN concentrations $2$--$4$ times those in surface runoff and nitrate-N constituting $71$--$85\%$ of TN \parencite{Bechmann2014}. New Zealand mole-pipe systems captured about $62\%$ of surplus rainfall as drainage and routed roughly $80\%$ of soluble N, while surface runoff dominated P, sediment, and \emph{E.\ coli} \parencite{Monaghan2016}. At watershed scale, tile drainage accounted for $56\%$ of annual discharge and $44$--$82\%$ (mean $62\%$) of NO$_3$-N export in Ohio **[CITATION CHECKED: Williams2015]**, averaged $57\%$ of streamflow and dominated nitrate export in Indiana \parencite{Grose2022}, and in Iowa the largest drains contributed $70$--$87\%$ of exported water and nitrate \parencite{Coupe2020}. In flat Illinois terrain, subsurface stations lost $13$--$30$~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ of nitrate-N ($16$--$26\%$ of applied N), with more than $70\%$ of samples exceeding the $10$~mg~L$^{-1}$ maximum contaminant level (MCL), while surface runoff was negligible \parencite{Dattamudi2020}.

subsection: Preferential Flow, Macroporosity, and Drainage-Induced Soil Structure
claim_paragraph: These structural findings manifest as rapid, connectivity-limited preferential transport. Conservative tracers reach drains within minutes to hours: chloride breakthrough increased by factors of $20$--$400$ within hours \parencite{Villholth1998}; bromide appeared within $1$~h yet cumulative capture was slow ($8\%$ in $48$~h, $\sim95\%$ only after months) \parencite{Frey2012,Kladivko2023}. Liquid-manure constituents reached drains within $5$~min, and soluble P moved through artificial macropores with little sorption, identifying macropore flow as the primary rapid-P mechanism \parencite{Stamm2002,Geohring2001}. These behaviours are captured only by models representing two-domain flow or a direct macropore--drain connection: a two-dimensional mobile--immobile model matched bromide dynamics far better than single-porosity formulations \parencite{Köhne2006}; adding a macropore domain was essential to match drainage chloride \parencite{Villholth1998b}; an ``express fraction'' of $\sim2\%$ reproduced immediate tracer breakthrough in RZWQM **[CITATION CHECKED: Fox2007b]**; and a macropore subroutine in APEX raised DRP-load performance from unsatisfactory to very good, with median annual macropore-flow and macropore-P contributions of $48\%$ and $43\%$ \parencite{Ford2017}. Fine-textured soils generated more macropore flow than coarse-textured soils, so soil texture explained connectivity-driven seasonal variation in flow partitioning \parencite{Poon2021,Holbak2021}.

subsection: Temporal Dynamics of Phosphorus and Sediment Loss
claim_paragraph: Preferential flow reconciles substantial subsurface PP loss with the filtering expected of matrix flow. $^{137}$Cs tracing shows drainage particulate matter originates from topsoil (median grain sizes $2$--$5$~$\mu$m) translocated within hours **[CITATION CHECKED: Laubel1999]**, and PP loss is episodic---nearly one-third of annual PP loss occurred during sampled storms \parencite{Laubel1999,Grant1996}. Because of this episodicity, discrete sampling underestimated annual P loss by $26\%$ to $>100\%$ \parencite{Grant1996}. At catchment scale, source-fingerprinting attributed $28$--$55\%$ of sediment yield to field drains, with topsoil supplying $70.9$--$88.6\%$ of the load and drains contributing over $50\%$ of the annual sediment budget in one catchment \parencite{Walling2002,Chapman2005}.

subsection: Soil Controls on Phosphorus Release and Legacy Phosphorus
claim_paragraph: Dissolved P loss is tightly coupled to soil P status. Loss in surface runoff and drainage related strongly to soil P content ($r^2 = 0.85$--$0.96$ for surface, $0.86$ for subsurface) \parencite{Sharpley1995}, and higher soil-test P (STP) raised DRP in both tiles and runoff \parencite{Osterholz2020}. Threshold behaviour is common: a change point in STP marks where extractable P and DRP rise more steeply \parencite{McDowell2001b}, and rainfall sharply increased subsurface DRP where STP exceeded $41$~mg~kg$^{-1}$ \parencite{Ni2020}. Where soils sorb P weakly, dissolved losses rise: A-horizon degree of P saturation (DPS) alone explained $83\%$ of tile TP variance, rising to $95$--$96\%$ with water-extractable P and sorption grouping \parencite{Beauchemin2003}, and a DPS threshold near $0.25$ predicted sandy-soil SRP \parencite{Siemens2004}. The highest-leaching profiles combined large labile topsoil P pools with low-sorption subsoils, so subsoil characteristics must be included in risk assessment **[CITATION CHECKED: Liu2024b]**. Subsurface P losses are generally small in fine-textured soils at moderate STP but become significant in sandy, organic, and very high-P soils from long-term fertilisation or manuring \parencite{Sims1998}. Sequential fractionation links pools to loss, with P lost to water associated with short-term ($<24$~h) exchangeable pools tied to Al, Fe, and Ca \parencite{McDowell2001}.

subsection: Phosphorus Loss Pathways and Water Partitioning
claim_paragraph: Tile drainage commonly captures the largest share of field water export: subsurface discharge accounted for $81\pm23\%$ of annual discharge in the Eastern Corn Belt \parencite{Pease2018} and $78$--$90\%$ in Ontario \parencite{VanEsbroeck2016}, and installing drainage re-routes water from surface- to drainage-dominated flow \parencite{Turtola1995,BENGTSON1995}. A recurring distinction is that surface runoff usually carries higher P \emph{concentrations} whereas tile drainage---carrying more water---can dominate annual \emph{loads}. In Ohio, flow-weighted DRP and TP concentrations were greater in surface runoff, yet subsurface discharge supplied $71\%$ of DRP and $69\%$ of TP load \parencite{Pease2018}; the same contrast appears in long-term Swedish monitoring \parencite{Norberg2022}. Tiles exported $40$--$77\%$ of TP and $19$--$67\%$ of DRP load in Ontario \parencite{VanEsbroeck2016}, $21$--$52\%$ of TP in Wisconsin \parencite{Madison2014}, and $65.4\%$ of annual TP at a southern-Ontario field **[CITATION CHECKED: Qi2018]**. Models corroborate the partitioning, attributing $66\%$ of DRP and $76\%$ of TP loss to subsurface drainage against observed $70\%$ and $80\%$ \parencite{Grewal2025,Sadhukhan2019b}.

subsection: Preferential Flow, Macroporosity, and Drainage-Induced Soil Structure
claim_paragraph: Two organising gradients recur: macroporosity and biopore abundance decline sharply with depth, whereas lateral variation relative to the drain is real but weaker. In a Finnish clay, macroporosity fell strongly with depth but differed little with distance, though earthworm burrows were $44\%$ more numerous above a drain and field saturated conductivity varied with drain position \parencite{Alakukku2010,Frey2011}. Reviews report higher infiltration and lower bulk density above drain lines and runoff reductions of $34$--$55\%$ relative to undrained soils \parencite{Montagne2009}. Sustained drainage consistently lowers bulk density and raises air-filled porosity and gaseous diffusivity: Ohio drainage decreased bulk density and increased air-filled pores \parencite{HUNDAL1976}, and relative gas-diffusion gains correlated with corn yield \parencite{Nakajima2014}. Consistent with an aeration mechanism, drainage raised soil oxygen, mineralisation, and nitrification \parencite{GROFFMAN1984}, and dynamic aeration indicators outperformed static bulk density in explaining productivity across a large Canadian survey \parencite{Caron2025}. The effect is context-dependent, however: some comparisons found lower bulk density under undrained or subirrigated soils \parencite{LAL1993,Baker2004}, drainage reduced surface organic matter and soil organic carbon in some Ohio studies \parencite{FAUSEY1992,Kumar2014}, and in the most compacted soils aeration control by drainage becomes impossible **[CITATION CHECKED: SMEDEMA1993]**.

subsection: Cover Crops: Reductions, Mechanisms, and Yield
claim_paragraph: Rye cover cropping generally imposes no consistent yield penalty, especially for soybean \parencite{Strock2004,Waring2020,Qi2011b}, with projected-climate differences of only $\sim0.1$~Mg~ha$^{-1}$ and no continuous-corn penalty in simulation \parencite{Malone2020,Birru2023}. Documented exceptions concentrate in maize, drought years, and silage---a $6\%$ average maize reduction (34\% in 2012) \parencite{MartinezFeria2016} and $16\%$ lower corn silage after manured rye \parencite{Krueger2013}. In harvested-rye systems, fertilizing the rye boosts biomass and energy with only a small N-loss cost \parencite{Malone2018,Malone2023}. section: In-Field Nutrient and Cropping Management
subsection: Nitrogen Rate, Source, and Residual Soil Nitrate
claim_paragraph: Drainage nitrate loss rising with N application rate is the most consistently documented in-field relationship, and it is paired with a yield plateau near the economic optimum. In Iowa production fields, yearly nitrate mass loss was greater for high- than for medium- and low-N treatments, with concentrations of $5$--$45$~mg~N~L$^{-1}$ \parencite{Jaynes2001}; four-year losses ranged $22$--$68$~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ and rose with rate in both continuous corn and corn--soybean \parencite{Helmers2012b}. Increasing N above the agronomic optimum yields diminishing returns: at $168$--$252$~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ in Illinois maize yield differed little while cumulative loads were statistically similar \parencite{Li2023b}, echoing early Iowa work that identified a single $150$~kg~ha$^{-1}$ application as a favorable compromise \parencite{Azevedo1997}; a $10\%$ rate cut lowered yield without significantly reducing loss at one site, underscoring site and hydrologic dependence \parencite{Gentry2024}. Regional syntheses formalize the pattern: maize yield followed a quadratic response peaking near $193$~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ while drainage N loss increased exponentially with rate, and yield-scaled loss rose sharply once N surplus exceeded $\sim23$~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$, identifying zero surplus as a practical target \parencite{Zhao2016}. N rate was the strongest predictor of annual concentration ($R^2=0.59$) with no yield gain above $150$--$224$~kg~ha$^{-1}$ **[CITATION CHECKED: Hertzberger2019]**, the most cost-effective high-rate scenarios also produced the highest losses \parencite{Liu2021}, and across syntheses each unit rise in rate produced $\sim0.12$~kg~NO$_3^-$-N loss, rate explaining $27\%$ of variability \parencite{Chatterjee2020b,Christianson2015b,Ritter2015}.

section: In-Field Nutrient and Cropping Management
subsection: Crop Rotation, Diversification, and Perennial Systems
claim_paragraph: Perennial and prairie systems are the most effective in-field option. Prairie concentrations were $\le1.4$~mg~L$^{-1}$, $2$--$195$ times below row crops \parencite{Daigh2015b}; restored prairie grass reduced losses to near rainfall levels \parencite{HernandezRamirez2011}; and alfalfa and CRP plots had $0.3$--$4$ versus $14$--$40$~mg~L$^{-1}$ for row crops, with four-year losses of $\sim200$~kg~ha$^{-1}$ for corn versus $4$--$7$ for perennials \parencite{Randall2001,Waring2024}. The benefit can be short-lived on conversion back to row crops as RSN rises **[CITATION CHECKED: Huggins2001]**. Converting corn--soybean area to alfalfa or wheatgrass reduced watershed losses $78$--$81\%$ \parencite{Wilson2023}, and bioenergy perennials also reduce loss \parencite{Ferin2023,Woodbury2018,Guo2018}. Diversified rotations, cover crops, and perennials are recognized as complementary reducers \parencite{Dinnes2002}.

section: In-Field Nutrient and Cropping Management
subsection: Nitrogen Timing, Placement, and Enhanced-Efficiency Products
claim_paragraph: Split, side-dress, and placement effects are mixed. Split fertilization reduced export only at lower rates \parencite{Liu2021} and was not significantly different from non-split in a continental synthesis \parencite{Hertzberger2019}; side-dress at V2--V12 gave no consistent difference \parencite{Jaynes2013}, and midseason splits sometimes raised concentration and RSN **[CITATION CHECKED: Jaynes2006]**. Split-applied urea modestly improved water quality \parencite{Waring2022}, and remote-sensing variable-rate side-dress averaged a $40\%$ reduction over 15 years, mainly via $33\%$ lower input and avoidance of peak flow, while maintaining yield \parencite{Wilson2020b}. Placement was inconsistent: injection and incorporation sometimes had higher concentrations than surface application \parencite{Hertzberger2019}, and a localized-compaction applicator gave $16\%$ lower concentrations than a spoke injector \parencite{Bakhsh2010}. Among enhanced-efficiency products, nitrapyrin generally did not reduce nitrate or improve yield alone \parencite{Vetsch2019,Pittelkow2017} but reduced fall-N losses $10$--$18\%$ in Minnesota rotations \parencite{Randall2003,Randall2005}; polymer-coated products were more robust, with ESN lowering combined N$_2$O, NH$_3$, and NO$_3^-$ losses $47$--$49\%$ below urea while maintaining yield, the largest benefit in wet periods \parencite{Menegaz2025,Nash2015,Nash2015b}. Reduced-rate summer fertigation cut concentration and load $\sim16\%$ without reducing silage yield \parencite{Gamble2018}, and fall anhydrous ammonia with nitrapyrin matched spring application environmentally \parencite{Kaur2024,Kaur2024c}.

section: In-Field Nutrient and Cropping Management
subsection: Soil Testing, Use Efficiency, Regional Aggregation, and Loss-Pathway Tradeoffs
claim_paragraph: Watershed-scale soil-test-based programs confirm in-field mechanisms at landscape scale. Adopting the late-spring nitrate test (LSNT) across a 400-ha Iowa subbasin reduced concentration by at least $30\%$ via reduced fertilizer use while matching yields \parencite{Jaynes2004,Karlen2005,Malone2010}, and soil-test programs generally reduced RSN and loss versus yield-goal management \parencite{Dinnes2002,Ritter2015}. Alternative farming practices reduced drainage $41\%$ and concentration from $17.2$ to $8.2$~mg~L$^{-1}$, cutting losses $59$--$62\%$ **[CITATION CHECKED: Oquist2007]**, and because $85\%$ of a Minnesota watershed's load came from tile drainage, substantial perennialization was needed for a $30$--$50\%$ reduction \parencite{Wilson2023,Makhtoumi2025}. Use efficiency framing is increasingly emphasized: partial factor productivity was highest for side-dress and lowest for very high fall N \parencite{Jaynes2015}, and EONR is proposed as a sustainability standard \parencite{Bandura2025}; adoption of cover crops, controlled drainage, and bioreactors remains constrained by financial and social barriers \parencite{David2015}.

section: In-Field Nutrient and Cropping Management
subsection: Tillage and Residue Management
claim_paragraph: Tillage exerts weak and inconsistent control over drainage nitrate relative to precipitation, cropping system, and N rate. Over 11 Minnesota years drain flow was higher under no-till but nitrate losses only slightly higher under conventional tillage, and moldboard-plow and no-till losses were similar ($43$ and $41$~kg~ha$^{-1}$), cropping system mattering far more \parencite{RANDALL1995,Randall2001}. In Iowa no-till and ridge-till usually had the lowest losses but rotation had greater influence **[CITATION CHECKED: Weed1996]**, regional syntheses found no significant tillage difference in N load \parencite{Zhao2016}, and conservation tillage had the highest concentration ($16.1$~mg~L$^{-1}$) \parencite{Hertzberger2019,Wang2016b}. Where reduced tillage builds soil health its nitrate effect remains equivocal: no-till lowered loads only in some water years and reduced yields \parencite{Masri2024}, though it raised soil organic carbon and lowered EONR \parencite{Cassman2025,Waring2024}. Residue and stover management had limited effect on nitrate: $50\%$ stover harvest reduced simulated loss only $1.1$~kg~ha$^{-1}$ \parencite{Malone2019}, residue removal had little impact on concentration or yield \parencite{Dougherty2020,Guo2018}, and continuous corn with residue removal plus rye achieved losses similar to other row crops \parencite{Daigh2015b,Farahani2020}.

section: Drainage Design and Water-Table Management
subsection: Controlled Drainage and Drainage Water Management
claim_paragraph: The mechanism is consistently one of flow--load coupling: syntheses report drainage water management reducing tile flow by $\sim46\%$ and nitrate loads by $\sim45$--$48\%$ \emph{mainly by reducing discharge rather than by enhancing denitrification}, which plays only a secondary role \parencite{Ross2016,Ward2018}. Two trade-offs qualify the benefit. First, because reduction operates through volume, drainage management often fails to lower nitrate \emph{concentrations} even where it lowers loads \parencite{Grenon2023,Wesström2014}. Second, CD can increase surface DRP and TP that partly offset subsurface benefits \parencite{King2022,Wu2025}. Timing is decisive: DRAINMOD analysis identified early March as the most effective control window (reductions up to $100\%$) whereas April starts resembled free drainage \parencite{Kesicka2023c}. Greenhouse-gas responses are mixed but generally not adverse **[CITATION CHECKED: Madramootoo2024]**.

section: Drainage Design and Water-Table Management
subsection: Enhanced Configurations and Persistence under Climate Change
claim_paragraph: A robust and management-relevant finding is that the benefits of controlled drainage persist, and in some seasons strengthen, under projected climates. In Ohio, conventional discharge was projected to decline while CD annual reductions remained near $4$--$6\%$ and summer growing-season reductions increased, indicating greater warm-season value \parencite{Pease2017}. Michigan simulations projected free-drainage discharge rising $20\%$ by mid-century while CD continued to reduce discharge by $63$--$72\%$, with future and historical performance statistically indistinguishable \parencite{BinShokrana2023}. Finnish scenarios projected CD effects remaining similar to the historical interval \parencite{Salla2022}, and Canadian projections of warmer, wetter conditions found CD reducing subsurface drainage more strongly than free drainage, though rising temperature drove dry-stress yield reductions that motivate the capture, storage, and reuse of drainage water **[CITATION CHECKED: Ndulue2024]**. Chinese and Polish studies likewise found that appropriate outlet-blocking strategies could reduce future runoff and maintain groundwater at present levels \parencite{Awad2021,Sojka2020}. Together these results indicate that the flow--load coupling underpinning water-table management is durable: because controlled systems act on discharge, their proportional benefits carry forward into a wetter, warmer future.

section: Drainage Design and Water-Table Management
subsection: Drainage Water Recycling and Subirrigation
claim_paragraph: Subirrigation---delivering water upward through the drains---similarly lowers losses and stabilises supply. It reduced soil-profile nitrate by up to $50\%$ and drainage nitrate concentrations by $55$--$73\%$, with water-quality benefits accruing even when outflow occasionally exceeded free drainage, implicating enhanced denitrification \parencite{Elmi2004,Elmi2002,Noory2009}. CDSI raised groundwater levels, supplied $170$--$410$~mm of infiltration, and increased Dutch yields by up to $64\%$ \parencite{deWit2022,deWit2024,FAUSEY1995,Almen2021,Madramootoo2007}. Its performance, however, is strongly site-dependent, governed by lateral hydraulic conductivity: across three Ohio sites subirrigation improved relative yield to $87$--$93\%$ and $80$--$91\%$ at two sites but had almost no effect at Defiance owing to very low conductivity \parencite{Gunn2018,Gunn2019}. Where hydraulics are favourable, CD and subirrigation kept soil water optimal in both wet and dry years \parencite{Niaghi2019}, and in claypan soybean systems subirrigation improved yield, reduced interannual variability, and allowed earlier planting **[CITATION CHECKED: Nelson2011]**; combining drainage water management with foliar pyraclostrobin produced synergistic soybean gains up to $1070$~kg~ha$^{-1}$ \parencite{Nelson2011b}.

section: Drainage Design and Water-Table Management
subsection: Drain Spacing and Depth as Controls on Flow and Loss
claim_paragraph: These relationships motivate an optimum-intensity principle: use the minimum subsurface intensity required to relieve excess-water stress, fit the system to the soil, and apply water-table control where maximum intensity is unnecessary \parencite{Breve1998}. Deeper drains often raise profit but substantially increase nitrate losses, and simulation showed that widening spacing to $100$~m cut total nitrate-N loss by $20\%$ ($37$ to $29$~kg~ha$^{-1}$) at small profit cost \parencite{ElSadek2002b,Breve1998}; deep drains are frequently unnecessary for salinity control \parencite{Ritzema2011}. A multi-state analysis found shallow drains gave quicker water-table drawdown, reduced yield variability, and $3.4$~cm less total flow than deep drains, though with more surface runoff and a lower benefit--cost ratio \parencite{Ghane2021b}, and field comparisons found shallow systems had the lowest nitrate concentration and loading among configurations, sometimes at a yield penalty whereas controlled drainage trended toward higher yields **[CITATION CHECKED: Smith2011b]**.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment, Reactive Media, and Watershed-Scale Integration
subsection: Woodchip bioreactors: performance, controls, and mechanisms
claim_paragraph: Denitrification is firmly established as the dominant pathway, accounting for $>98\%$ of transformed nitrate in microcosms, with immobilisation and DNRA minor \parencite{Greenan2006,Greenan2009}. Woodchip carbon sustains this capacity for years: wood raised denitrification potential $31$- to $4000$-fold over subsoil, supported denitrifier populations $>10^8$~g$^{-1}$, and gave in situ nitrate half-lives of $0.64$--$0.81$~d \parencite{Moorman2010}; DNRA and anammox occur secondarily \parencite{Hartfiel2022,Mendes2021}. Cellulose is the most rapidly consumed compound, and wood decomposition is depth-dependent (up to $75\%$ loss near the inlet/top, $<13\%$ at depth), governing longevity \parencite{Hartfiel2022,Moorman2010,Ghane2018}. Alternative substrates can raise performance: corncob (CC75) removed more N than woodchips ($61.2\%$ vs $37.9\%$) at lowest cost \parencite{Law2023}, corn-stover blends enhanced removal \parencite{Oladeji2023}, and agricultural residues can outperform woodchips for removal though woodchips give better hydraulics \parencite{Greenan2006,Kohn2023,Zhang2021b}. Communities are shaped by substrate, depth, season, and temperature \parencite{Hartfiel2022}, with cold-active denitrifiers (\textit{Cellulomonas}, \textit{Pseudomonas}) and nitrate-reducing fungi identified as key taxa **[CITATION CHECKED: Aldossari2021]**; bioaugmentation shows conditional promise but is limited by washout \parencite{Jeglot2022,Wang2025b}, and denitrification function is generally robust to water-level disturbance \parencite{Hathaway2017}.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment, Reactive Media, and Watershed-Scale Integration
subsection: Woodchip bioreactors: performance, controls, and mechanisms
claim_paragraph: The dominant, repeatedly quantified control is HRT, which trades off against the fraction of flow captured: efficiency rises with HRT \parencite{Bell2015,Rivas2020}, while in the ten-bioreactor dataset annual flow-weighted HRT correlated with flow captured ($\rho=-0.67$) and treated-water removal efficiency ($\rho=0.60$) \parencite{Christianson2026}. Column work shows removal rate per unit wood rising with flow while efficiency falls \parencite{Greenan2009}, and higher influent loads raise the removal \emph{rate} but lower percentage efficiency **[CITATION CHECKED: Christianson2026]**. Temperature exerts a strong, consistent effect: exponential functions of water temperature and HRT explained $73\%$ of the variance in load reduction in Illinois \parencite{Bell2015}; South Dakota removal fell $\sim30\%$ below $12\,^{\circ}$C \parencite{Thapa2023}; columns dropped from $96\%$ at $21.5\,^{\circ}$C to $29\%$ at $10\,^{\circ}$C \parencite{Soupir2018}; and Michaelis--Menten $V_{max}$ fell sharply from $22$ to $5\,^{\circ}$C \parencite{Kouanda2021,Zhang2021b}. Kinetically, removal is zero-order when nitrate is non-limiting and shifts to first-order once nitrate becomes limiting \parencite{Hua2016,Kouanda2021}.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment, Reactive Media, and Watershed-Scale Integration
subsection: Constructed wetlands
claim_paragraph: Constructed wetlands treating drainage are extensively documented nitrate sinks in which denitrification dominates. Across French watersheds, nitrate removal averaged $\sim42\%$, of which denitrification supplied $93\%$, and devoting $\sim1\%$ of the contributing area can achieve $50\%$ removal, with hydraulic residence time the priority design control \parencite{Tournebize2017}. Field systems span a coherent range: Iowa wetlands reduced incoming nitrate $49\%$ \parencite{Drake2018}, a Minnesota wetland removed $67\%$ over four years **[CITATION CHECKED: Gordon2021]**, and Illinois wetlands retained $36$--$37\%$ of N, implying $\sim450$~ha to cut watershed N loading $46\%$ \parencite{Kovacic2006}. Broader syntheses place average total-N removal near $39\%$ \parencite{Wang2025b}, with roughly $40$--$50\%$ N removal generally achievable at wetland-to-catchment area ratios of $1$--$4\%$ and only minor gains beyond \parencite{Mendes2021}. Because performance is a strong function of hydraulic loading, residence time, temperature, and inlet concentration, no single-number design is adequate, and higher influent loads raise removal \emph{rate} but lower percentage efficiency \parencite{Kadlec2012,Steidl2019,Mendes2021}. Nitrate removal is reliable, but phosphorus performance is variable and wetlands sometimes export more TP than they receive \parencite{Tanner2005,Tanner2011,Messer2021}, with plant harvest an important P route in some systems \parencite{Lenhart2016}. Paired surface-flow wetland plus woodchip systems act as consistent nutrient sinks (TN removal $8$--$51\%$, TP $0$--$80\%$), the woodchip component contributing more removal than the sedimentation basin while occupying a smaller footprint than a standalone wetland \parencite{Pugliese2020}.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment, Reactive Media, and Watershed-Scale Integration
subsection: Comparative effectiveness, cost, and watershed-scale integration
claim_paragraph: Because tile drainage is the primary pathway controlling watershed water and nitrogen export, downstream targets translate to large required reductions at the tile outlet---about $55\%$ for one Iowa river \parencite{Schilling2012b,Ikenberry2014}. Concentrations decline with drainage area as export dilutes downstream, and substantial in-network retention ($34$--$82\%$) occurs via underground denitrification, though in-stream processing immediately below tile outlets offers little potential because its timing is poorly matched to seasonal loading \parencite{Schilling2012b,Billy2011,Billy2013}. This scale attenuation of in-field effects means edge-of-field benefits measured at a single tile can be diluted at the watershed outlet, and meeting large goals requires \emph{combining} in-field and edge-of-field practices. In the Mississippi basin, nitrogen-management practices alone were insufficient, but N-management plus N-removal practices reached the $45\%$ target while converting under $6\%$ of cropland when targeted \parencite{McLellan2015}, and LiDAR-based placement achieved $34$--$39\%$ nitrate reduction while removing $<5\%$ of cropland **[CITATION CHECKED: Kvítek2023]**. Long-term records confirm that stacked BMPs work, with Czech outlet nitrate declining over 2004--2018 and combined practices cutting load $60.3\%$ \parencite{Fraindová2022,Law2022}. Crucially, traditional surface-water BMPs can be inadequate over tile drainage: seven years of strip-till, grassed waterways, and stream buffers produced no measurable change in nitrate, phosphorus, sediment, or hydrology because they did not intercept subsurface flow, which must therefore be a design priority \parencite{Lemke2011}. Finally, monitoring design strongly affects inferred loads: high-frequency sampling captures storm dynamics that grab sampling misses, and significant nitrate declines are far more detectable in flow-weighted concentration than in load or yield \parencite{Drake2018,Danalatos2022,Irvine2019}.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment, Reactive Media, and Watershed-Scale Integration
subsection: Reactive media for phosphorus removal
claim_paragraph: Iron-based materials are the best-performing class, routinely removing $\geq95\%$ of phosphate in batch and $>90\%$ in most columns with negligible desorption \parencite{Allred2014,Allred2012,Allred2017,Mendes2022}. Iron filings reached the highest capacity of $4.95$~mg~g$^{-1}$ and steel slag $1.68$~mg~g$^{-1}$, versus only $0.10$--$0.13$~mg~g$^{-1}$ for natural minerals---an order-of-magnitude advantage for industrial by-products \parencite{Sellner2019b}. Granular iron-oxide media retained SRP below detection far longer than steel by-products \parencite{Hauda2020}, Fe-based CFH media were most robust under variable flow \parencite{Pugliese2023}, and iron-activated alumina reached $94.4\%$ removal \parencite{Kumari2025}. Ca-rich slag and cement-kiln blends achieve $>98\%$ removal at low-to-moderate loading \parencite{Agrawal2011,Sanford2016}, and lime-amended fly-ash pellets reached $1.98$~mg~P~g$^{-1}$ \parencite{Li2017}, but their performance is governed by a finite supply of reactive $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$: phosphorus is removed in a moving front as $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and pH-buffering capacity are consumed, downstream slag being more efficient than upstream \parencite{Wang2020d}, and field removal collapses once treated-water pH falls below $8.5$, with $100\%$ removal sustained only to $\sim500$~mg~P~kg$^{-1}$ slag \parencite{Penn2020}. Consistent with the two mechanisms, lower pH favours Fe-based adsorption whereas higher pH favours Ca-based precipitation **[CITATION CHECKED: Mendes2022]**, and finer particle sizes and coexisting-ion chemistry (sulfate, bicarbonate, and DOC reduce uptake) modulate performance \parencite{Li2020,Sellner2019b,Pugliese2023}. Natural minerals such as zeolite give lower, modest removal ($21$--$58\%$) unless modified \parencite{Agrawal2011,Sadeghi2021}.

section: Edge-of-Field Treatment, Reactive Media, and Watershed-Scale Integration
subsection: Saturated buffers, denitrification walls, ditches, and in-channel practices
claim_paragraph: In-channel and edge structures add interception where drains discharge. Saturated riparian buffers, which redistribute tile flow laterally through the riparian soil, offer the largest climate-mitigation potential per unit area among conservation-drainage practices \parencite{Hall2025}. Riparian zones remove nitrate efficiently by denitrification---groundwater nitrate fell from $7$--$8$ to $<0.1$~mg~L$^{-1}$ within $16$--$47$~m \parencite{JACOBS1985,Schilling2022}---and redirecting tile flow into a buffer removed nitrate at $1.01\pm0.07$~mg~N~L$^{-1}$~m$^{-1}$, with chloride confirming denitrification rather than dilution \parencite{Jaynes2014,Carstensen2021}. Across six saturated buffers, all removed nitrate from tile-outlet water ($13$--$179$~kg~N~yr$^{-1}$ over $3.4$--$40.5$~ha; $8$--$84\%$ effectiveness) at a mean cost of US\$$2.94$~kg$^{-1}$~N, making them simple, cheap, and quick to install \parencite{Jaynes2019}. Denitrification beds followed Michaelis--Menten kinetics with very low greenhouse-gas emissions \parencite{Ghane2015}. In-channel practices contribute additional reductions: a low-grade weir cut nitrate load $58\%$ \parencite{Strock2025b}, a two-stage ditch reduced TP load $40\%$ \parencite{Hodaj2017}, and blind inlets and subsurface fertiliser placement reduced DRP $65$--$72\%$ \parencite{Kröger2013,Wilson2019,Sharpley2019}. Stacking practices multiplies benefit: a combined drainage-management--bioreactor--saturated-buffer system reduced nitrate export $78$--$88\%$ **[CITATION CHECKED: Singh2024b]**. A key limit is that where tile drains route water directly to streams they bypass the riparian zone, curtailing natural attenuation \parencite{Puckett2005}.

section: Other Water-Quality Dimensions: Pesticides, Microbes, Trace Elements, and Greenhouse Gases
subsection: Herbicides, Pesticides, and Emerging Contaminants
claim_paragraph: The mechanism reconciling near-immediate arrival with small overall losses is preferential (macropore) flow. Tracer breakthrough curves were typical of preferential flow, with herbicides arriving after less than $1$~cm of net drainage, interpreted as transport through only $\sim3\%$ of pore volume \parencite{Fortin2002,Dousset2004}. Soil structure, rather than sorption or degradation, dominated between-soil differences, with greater metolachlor losses in a clayey Vertic Cambisol than a loamy Luvisol \parencite{Novak2001,Novak2003}. Although mass losses are small, transient concentrations can exceed thresholds: Ontario maxima reached $287$~$\mu$g~L$^{-1}$ (atrazine) in tile discharge, with the atrazine MCL exceeded in $60\%$ of tile samples \parencite{GAYNOR1995}, and Iowa subsurface drains had glyphosate maxima above $250$~$\mu$g~L$^{-1}$ \parencite{Coupe2012}. Degradates contribute meaningfully and can be more mobile than parents: deethylatrazine accounted for $10$--$27\%$ of combined loss \parencite{GAYNOR1995,MUIR1978,JAYACHANDRAN1994}. Management levers include banding, residue-conserving tillage with intercrops (reducing loss $46$--$49\%$), and application-timing restriction via a soil-wetness index \parencite{Gaynor2001,Julien2023,Moorman1999}, whereas corn-stover harvest can worsen drainage quality \parencite{Shipitalo2016}. Woodchip and biochar-amended bioreactors removed atrazine (up to $93\%$) mainly abiotically without inhibiting denitrification \parencite{Hassanpour2019,Ilhan2011}, and modelling frameworks (PESTDRAIN, HYDRUS-2D, RZWQM, SWAT+) reproduce drainage pesticide dynamics when macroporosity and sorption kinetics are represented **[CITATION CHECKED: Branger2009]**. Tile drainage also transports emerging contaminants---PPCPs, hormones, PBDEs, perfluoroalkyl acids, and neonicotinoids---whose behaviour mirrors the timing and preferential-flow patterns above, generally at low, transient concentrations \parencite{Gottschall2012,Gottschall2013,Gottschall2017,Ghirardini2019,Schaafsma2019}.

section: Other Water-Quality Dimensions: Pesticides, Microbes, Trace Elements, and Greenhouse Gases
subsection: Trace Elements, Selenium, and Acid Sulphate Hazards
claim_paragraph: Where drainage concentrates trace elements, it can create acute ecological hazards. The Kesterson Reservoir remains the definitive case: waterborne selenium averaged $0.122$~mg~L$^{-1}$ ($\sim230$ times reference), biomagnified through the food chain, and caused dead and deformed bird embryos, with integrated studies fulfilling the equivalent of Koch's postulates and identifying selenium as the sole causative agent \parencite{SAIKI1987,Ohlendorf2002,BENSON1993}. The regulatory legacy is durable: open-water evaporation is now prohibited in California, requiring rock-media systems \parencite{Ayars2014,BRADFORD1991}, and selenium-removal wetlands retained about $59\%$ of inflow Se \parencite{Gao2003}. In evaporation basins, evapoconcentration accumulates extreme salinity and trace elements \parencite{WESTCOT1988}, and redox chemistry jointly controls arsenic and uranium mobility **[CITATION CHECKED: Gao2007]**; boron isotopes and other tracers can distinguish contaminant sources \parencite{Tayfur2010,Komor1997,Zhou2023}. At the opposite extreme, intensive drainage can drive negative micronutrient balances and net soil depletion \parencite{Gul2013}, while central-Iowa drainage ionic composition was dominated by bicarbonate, calcium, and magnesium \parencite{Zimmerman2017b}. Drainage of acid sulphate soils is a distinct hazard: oxidation of pyritic sediments drives stream pH declines to near or below $4.0$ and elevates aluminium and metals, with controlled pipe drainage recommended over in-stream liming \parencite{Osterholm2005,Åström2005,Virtanen2017,Salo2023}.
